headline: New-moon springs flush the bay — fluke and bass stack at the Moriches Inlet cut
subhead: Great South Bay water pushing into the high 70s has shoved the fluke out to the channels, and this weekend's new-moon tides are about to turn the inlet into a conveyor belt.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what bays do in the first week of July — it cooked. Great South Bay pushed into the high 70s, touching 78.8 in the shallow flats off Tuthill Point and East Moriches, and that kind of water doesn't hold fluke. It holds sea robins and bathtub-warm slop. What it did do was push every keeper fluke in the system toward cooler water, and in this system that means one of two places: the main channel through the bay or the inlet itself, where the ocean is still feeding in cleaner, cooler water on every tide. That migration is the single biggest story on my beat right now, and it's not subtle — guys who were picking at fluke on the flats two weeks ago are getting skunked there now and finding them stacked in the cut.

This week the moon does the rest of the work for us. We're building into new-moon springs, peak alignment landing right around July 11-13, which means bigger tidal range and more water moving through a system that's already narrow and touchy after last fall's shoaling. Moriches Inlet doesn't have the luxury of a wide throat like Shinnecock — every extra foot of tidal push gets squeezed through that cut and accelerates. That's good news if you're fishing structure. The outgoing on those spring tides is going to run harder and longer than it has in weeks, which flushes bait — spearing, small bunker, grass shrimp — out of the bay and stacks it against the sandbar off Cupsogue and the rock jetty on the Smith Point side. Predators know this. Stripers and blues will set up in the eddies behind the bar and let the current do their work for them.

The striper bite through the inlet itself has been steady, not spectacular — I'd call it a solid mid-tier week. Best window has consistently been the last two hours of the outgoing, fished tight to the west side of the cut where the deeper scour channel runs against the Cupsogue side. Bucktails in the 1- to 1.5-ounce range, white or chartreuse, worked slow along bottom in that 12- to 15-foot trench, have been drawing fish in the 24- to 32-inch range with the occasional better fish mixed in on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig right where the current breaks off the tip of the bar. Live eels after dark have also produced, particularly on the last of the outgoing into the start of the slack, fished off the rocks at the east jetty. Nothing has been a blitz. You're working for these fish, and on a lot of tides you're getting two or three fish in a session, not a dozen. That's honest — the bay isn't stuffed with bass right now, but the ones passing through the inlet on that flush are eating.

Fluke is where the real story is. With the bay fish pushed toward structure, the drift through the inlet channel itself — from the Coast Guard station down through the cut and out to the sea buoy — has been the most consistent producer on my beat. Four- and 5-inch white Gulp swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing in 15 to 25 feet, have taken fish to 6 pounds, with a good number of keepers mixed into a lot of short fish. The bite window tightens up around the last two hours of the outgoing and first hour of slack — once the tide turns and starts flooding back in, the fluke seem to lose interest and scatter. Ocean-side drifts off Cupsogue in that upwelled 71-degree water have also been worth the run, particularly for guys willing to work the deeper humps a quarter-mile off the beach.

Porgies have shown consistently at Pattersquash and in the deeper holes off Tuthill Point, standard high-low rigs with clam, nothing to write home about but a reliable box-filler if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — I haven't had a real report worth passing along. Water's been warm enough on paper for weeks now and the fish just haven't shown in numbers here, which tracks with what's happening system-wide. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

The development I'm watching closest is the pelagic push. The bonito and Spanish mackerel window that opened around the Fourth is in its final days, and the early signs are pointing at Moriches and Shinnecock on the ocean side picking up fish on clean incoming water. If you've got a boat that can work outside the bar, small metal jigs and Deadly Dicks worked fast around bait pods off Cupsogue on the incoming are worth a look through the weekend before that window likely closes.

Looking ahead: if the new-moon springs build the way the tide charts suggest, I'd be at the inlet cut Friday through Monday working the last two hours of the outgoing, bucktails for the fluke, chunks and eels for the bass in the deeper scour. If the current gets too strong to fish clean — and on a big spring tide through this pinched inlet, that's a real possibility — I'd shift inside to the flats around Tuthill Point on the front half of the incoming, where the bait gets pushed back in and the bass and fluke follow it. Either way, the water's moving with purpose this week. That's usually when this inlet gets interesting.
